paragraphs: Here's what I see, friend. Three kings, and the same question under all of them: what does it mean to know the LORD? The LORD answers it Himself through Jeremiah, and it has nothing to do with cedar. Of the king's father, He says, "He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?" (Jeremiah 22:16). Knowing God shows up in how you treat people, especially the ones who can't pay you back.

Now look at the son. He built a big palace and didn't pay the workers (Jeremiah 22:13). The LORD asks, "Does it make you a king to excel in cedar?" (Jeremiah 22:15). A nice house with crooked dealings underneath is still crooked. And I'll be honest, I know a little about being tempted to judge by the shiny outside. The LORD says He warned them when they felt secure, and they said, "I will not listen" (Jeremiah 22:21). That's a heavy part, and I think it hurts because comfort can make a heart stop listening.

So here's what I'm carrying out of this one. The LORD isn't impressed by crowns, a royal family tree or even a signet ring, because He says that even a signet ring on His right hand would not save Coniah from what was coming (Jeremiah 22:24). What He's looking for is a life that does right by people, and a heart that still listens when things are going fine. Check your own kitchen, baker. Who is your work helping, and who is it leaving unpaid? The story of these kings isn't over, but the lesson already stands: knowing God and doing justice go together.
